There are two forms: the [[inclusive or]] and the [[exclusive or]].}} # {{n-g|Used to present two or more options from which a choice is to be made.}} #: {{ux|en|Do you want tea '''or''' coffee?}} #: {{ux|en|You may stay '''or''' go.}} # [[otherwise|Otherwise]] {{gloss|a consequence of the condition that the previous is false}}. #: {{ux|en|It's raining! Come inside '''or''' you'll catch a cold!}} #* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=IV|page=46|passage=No matter how early I came down, I would find him on the veranda, smoking cigarettes, '''or''' otherwise his man would be there with a message to say that his master would shortly join me if I would kindly wait.}} # {{n-g|Connects two equivalent names.}} #: {{ux|en|The country [[Myanmar]], '''or''' [[Burma]]}} ## {{lb|en|archaic}} ''Used in the title of a work after a short name to introduce an alternative name, generally one which is more descriptive. Typically preceded by a semicolon or colon and followed by a comma.'' ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Isaac Newton|title={{w|Opticks|Opticks: '''or''', A Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light}}|year=1704|nocolon=1|page_plain=title page|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/opticksortreatisnewt/page/n8/mode/1up}} ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Eliza Haywood|title={{w|Love in Excess; or, The Fatal Enquiry|Love in Excess; '''or''' The Fatal Enquiry}}|year=1719|nocolon=1|page_plain=title page|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/loveinexcessorfa00hayw/page/n4/mode/1up}} ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Samuel Richardson|title={{w|Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded|Pamela; '''or''', Virtue Rewarded}}|year=1740|nocolon=1|page_plain=title page|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/richardsonpamela3ed04/page/n5/mode/1up}} ##* {{quote-book|en|author=w:Erasmus Darwin|title={{w|Zoonomia|Zoonomia; '''or''', the Laws of Organic Life}}|year=1794|nocolon=1|page_plain=title page|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/zoonomiaorlawsof1794darw/page/n4/mode/1up}} # {{n-g|Used in between two [[numbers]] to denote a [[range]] between them.}} #: {{ux|en|A man of 18 '''or''' 20 years}} =====Usage notes===== * {{s|connecting alternative terms}} When not implied by the meaning of the [[conjoin#Noun|conjoin]]s, it is generally ambiguous whether “or” is intended in an exclusive or inclusive sense. In speech, various means may be used to convey exclusivity, such as stress on the word “or” or a rising intonation before it.{{cite-book|en|last=Huddleston|first=Rodney|year=1988|title=English Grammar: An Outline|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0521311527|pages=198–99}} In a formal or technical register, {{m|en|and/or}} may be used to specify inclusivity. =====Derived terms===== an [[equilateral]] [[rectangle]]; a [[regular]] [[quadrilateral]]. #: {{hyper|en|rectangle#Noun|rhombus#Noun|kite#Noun|parallelogram#Noun|<|polygon#Noun|<|shape#Noun}} #: {{cot|en|circle|oval|triangle|trapezoid|lozenge|diamond}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1927|author=w:Kazimir Malevich|title=The Non-Objective World |passage=I took refuge in the square form and exhibited a picture which consisted of nothing more than a black '''square''' on a white field.}} # {{senseid|en|anything shaped like the polygon}} Something characterized by a [[#Adjective|square]], or nearly square, form. ## A {{l|en|cell}} in a {{l|en|grid}}. ##: {{ux|en|You may not move a piece to a '''square''' already occupied by one of your own pieces.}} ## A square piece, part, or surface. ##: {{ux|en|a square of '''glass'''}} ## The front of a woman's dress over the bosom, usually worked or embroidered. ## {{lb|en|North America}} A dessert cut into rectangular pieces, or a piece of such a dessert. ## {{lb|en|printing}} A certain number of lines, forming a portion of a [[column]], nearly square; used chiefly in reckoning the prices of advertisements in newspapers. ##: {{cot|en|column inch}} # {{senseid|en|tool}} An L- or T-shaped [[tool]] used to place objects or draw [[line]]s at [[right angle]]s. #: {{hypo|en|steel square|framing square|carpenter's square|T-square}} ## {{lb|en|figuratively|obsolete}} A true measure, standard, or pattern. # {{senseid|en|open space or park}} An open space or park, often in the center of a [[town]], not necessarily square in shape, often containing trees, seating and other features pleasing to the eye. #: {{syn|en|piazza|plaza}} #* {{RQ:Addison Italy |passage=The statue of Alexander the Seventh stands in the large '''square''' of the town.}} #* {{quote-av|en|date=October 10 1995|title=[[q:NewsRadio|NewsRadio]]|season=2|number=3 |passage=You're not in Wisconsin, Dave. ===Etymology 1===
{{PIE word|en|tréyes}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*peh₂ǵ-}}
{{rfc|en|Middle Scots comes after Middle English.}}
From {{inh|en|enm|travelen|t=to make a laborious journey, travel}} from {{der|en|gmw-msc|travailen|t=to toil, work, travel}}, alteration of {{cog|enm|travaillen|t=to toil, work}}, from {{der|en|fro|travailler|t=to trouble, suffer, be worn out}}. See the {{glossary|doublet}}s {{doublet|en|travail|travois|notext=1}}.

Compare typologically {{m|en|routine}} << {{m+|la|rupta via}}. Note the inverse semantic vectors: ''travel'' moves from a subjective state (toil) to an objective action (journey), while ''routine'' moves from an objective object (beaten path) to a subjective pattern (habit).

Largely displaced native {{m|en|fare}}, from {{cog|ang|faran|t=to go [a long distance], to travel}}. More at {{m|en|fare}}.

===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*terh₁-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|throwen}}, {{m|enm|thrawen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|þrāwan|t=to turn, twist}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*þrāan}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*þrēaną|t=to twist, turn}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*terh₁-|t=to rub, rub by twisting, twist, turn}}.

Cognate with {{cog|sco|thraw|t=to twist, turn, throw}}, {{cog|fy|triuwe|t=to push}}, {{cog|nl|draaien|t=to turn}}, {{cog|nds|draien}}, {{m|nds|dreien|t=to turn (in a lathe)}}, {{cog|de|drehen|t=to turn}}.

{{displaced|en|sl=1|warp}} as the word for hurling and was {{displaced|en|nocap=1|sl=1|by=1|warp}} as the word for twisting.

The use in computing comes from the fact, that in programming languages a statement reporting an error interrupts normal processing and sends an error object up the function calling stack until a handling statement intercepts it. Thus an “object” is “thrown” and “flies” until it is “caught”.

From {{inh|en|enm|hore}}, from {{inh|en|ang|hōre}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*hōrǭ}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*kéh₂ros|t=loved}}, from {{m|ine-pro|*keh₂-|t=to wish; desire}}. The unetymological spelling with ''wh-'' superficially denotes a formerly standard pronunciation with an excrescent {{IPAchar|/w/}} (such as in {{m|en|whole}}), but such a form is hardly found in either commentators on Early Modern English pronunciations or records of traditional dialects (which both explicitly mention its rarity or absence), therefore leaving the spelling somewhat inexplicable.<ref name="Dobson">{{R:en:Dobson:1957|II|430|998}}</ref> However, this may be because such an excrescent {{IPAchar|/w/}} was absorbed by a following {{IPAchar|/uː/}} (as in words with etymological {{IPAchar|/w/}} such as {{m|en|whom}}, {{m|en|two}}) after it became established in the spelling but before our earliest orthoepic records.

====Usage notes====
* The second meaning of {{m|en|refute||to deny the truth of}} is [[proscribed]] as [[erroneous]] by some [http://books.google.co.uk/books?id=2yJusP0vrdgC&pg=PA807&lpg=PA807&dq=english+usage+refute&source=web&ots=nYrYodyZZ4&sig=G_alFFyWi7ZFBMYnaujrrrh9qUM&hl=en&sa=X&oi=book_result&resnum=4&ct=result| (compare Merriam Webster,1994)]. An alternative term with such a meaning is {{m|en|repudiate}}, which means to reject or refuse to acknowledge, but without the implication of justification.
* ''Refute'' is also often confused with ''[[rebut]]''; a ''[[rebuttal]]'', in formal debate terms, is a counter-refutation, and it also has a specific legal sense, though like ''[[refutation]]'', the word has taken on the informal and disputed meaning of ''[[denial]]''.

Other linguists suggested that ''bull dyke(r)'' referred to strong black women who dug dikes, or derived from {{m|en|bull}} + {{m|en|dick}}, perhaps in reference to black men.Charles Panati, ''Sexy Origins and Intimate Things'' (1998), p. 181: "In fact, “bulldiking” is one of the earliest phrases in which the term “dike" has tough female overtones. It appeared in the American South in the nineteenth century, used by black Americans. Some linguists believe that strong black women who helped dig watercourses on Southern plantations were called “bulldikes.” Others, however, claim that "dike" is really a corruption of "dick", slang for "penis," and [...] argue that in the American South, black men who worked on plantations were called "bull dicks" by their white owners." It has also been suggested ''dyke'' is a shortening of {{m|en|morphodyke}}, from ''[[morphodite]]'', from ''[[hermaphrodite]]'',{{cite-book|en|year=1991|author=Sterling K. Eisiminger|title=The Consequence of Error and Other Language Essays|publisher=Peter Lang Pub Incorporated|text=Archibald Hill suggests that both dike and dyke are respectively clipped forms of morphodite and morphodyke, themselves clipped and mispronounced forms of hermaphrodite (A.S. 57.1).}} but the derivation may go in the other direction instead, with ''morphodyke'' being a blend of ''morphodite'' with the already-extant word ''dyke''. ====Noun==== {{en-noun}} {{tlb|en|slang|vulgar|usually|derogatory|and|offensive}} # {{sid|en|lesbian}} {{lb|en|anti-LGBTQ slur}} A [[lesbian]], particularly one with [[masculine]] or [[butch]] [[trait]]s or [[behavior]];
